Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR  

**MapLibre Native on Android cannot work without a `glyphs` URL, but you can make the *only* glyphs you need be a tiny local set (e.g. Latin only) and let every other script be drawn from device-installed fonts.**  

Do this by  

1. **Bundling the font files (TTF/OTF) you want to use** in your APK (`assets/fonts/…`).  
2. **Adding a `font-faces` block to your style** that points at those files with `file:///android_asset/...` URLs.  
3. **Pointing the style’s `glyphs` field at a local “dummy” glyph server** (a folder in `assets/glyphs/` that contains only the ranges you really need – usually the Latin range `0-255`).  
4. **Loading the style with `MapView` / `MapLibreMap`** exactly as you would for any offline style.  

The result:  

* All Latin text (or any range you actually ship) is taken from the tiny PBF files you bundled.  
* All other scripts (CJK, Arabic, Devanagari, etc.) are rendered by the native text-shaping engine (Harfbuzz) from the TTF/OTF files you supplied – no network request, no glyph-server traffic.  

Below is a step-by-step guide, plus the bits you need to copy-paste into your project.

---

## 1. Choose the fonts you want to use locally  

| Script | Recommended open-source font (covers the whole script) | Why you need it in `font-faces` |
|--------|--------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Latin / Greek / Cyrillic | **Noto Sans Regular** (or Roboto, Open Sans) | Most map labels are Latin; you can also ship the PBFs for this script, but it’s optional – the TTF works too. |
| Arabic / Hebrew | **Noto Sans Arabic** / **Noto Sans Hebrew** | These scripts need proper shaping; the TTF gives the correct glyphs and direction. |
| Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc. | **Noto Sans Devanagari**, **Noto Sans Thai**, … | HarfBuzz will shape them correctly when the TTF is available. |
| CJK (Chinese-Japanese-Korean) | **Noto Sans CJK SC/TC/JP/KR** (or any system CJK font) | Native does **not** have a `localIdeographFontFamily` fallback, so you must ship the TTF if you want CJK labels. |
| Any custom brand font | Your own `MyBrand-Regular.ttf` | Same mechanism – just add it to `font-faces`. |

> **Tip:** If you only need Latin labels, you can skip the `font-faces` entry for Latin and rely on the tiny glyph PBFs you’ll bundle (see step 3). The native engine will still fall back to the system “sans-serif” for any missing glyphs.

### Add the files to the APK  

Create the folder `src/main/assets/fonts/` (or `assets/` if you prefer the older Gradle layout) and copy the `.ttf`/`.otf` files there, e.g.:

```
app/
 └─ src/
     └─ main/
         └─ assets/
             ├─ fonts/
             │   ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf
             │   ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf
             │   ├─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf
             │   └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf
             └─ glyphs/          ← will hold the tiny PBF set (step 3)
```

Gradle automatically packages everything under `assets/` into the APK, and they are reachable at runtime via the `file:///android_asset/` scheme.

---

## 2. Add a `font-faces` block to your style JSON  

The `font-faces` property lives at the **root** of the style (outside `layers`, `sources`, etc.).  
Each key is the exact string you will use in `text-font` arrays.  
Each entry is an array of objects that describe the font file(s) and optional `unicode-range`s.

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Regular": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF"]   // Latin + basic punctuation
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Devanagari": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans CJK SC": [
      {
        "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF", "U+20000-2A6DF"]
      }
    ]
  },

  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": [
          "Noto Sans Regular",
          "Noto Sans Arabic",
          "Noto Sans Devanagari",
          "Noto Sans CJK SC"
        ],
        "text-size": 12
      },
      "paint": { "text-color": "#222" }
    }
  ]
}
```

**What this does**

* When the map needs a glyph for a code point that falls inside one of the `unicode-range`s, the native engine loads the TTF/OTF from the `url` and shapes the text with HarfBuzz.  
* If a code point is *outside* all declared ranges, the engine falls back to the `glyphs` URL (see next section).  

> **Important:** The `url` **must** be reachable by the native runtime. `file:///android_asset/...` works out-of-the-box on Android because MapLibre Native resolves that scheme to the APK’s assets. On iOS you would use `file://` pointing at the app bundle.

---

## 3. Provide a *minimal* glyph-PBF tree (offline “glyph server”)  

MapLibre Native **requires** a non-empty `glyphs` URL; if it is omitted the map will fail to load.  
You can satisfy the requirement with a **tiny** set of pre-generated PBF files that cover only the ranges you truly need (often just the basic Latin range).  

### 3.1 Generate the tiny set (once)

1. Install **font-maker** (the web UI is easiest) or use the CLI `fontnik`.  
2. Choose a font that you already ship (e.g. `NotoSans-Regular.ttf`).  
3. In the UI, set **Unicode ranges** to `0-255` (or any other range you want to pre-bundle).  
4. Export the resulting folder structure – it will look like:

```
glyphs/
 └─ Noto%20Sans%20Regular/
     ├─ 0-255.pbf
     └─ 256-511.pbf   (empty, you can delete)
```

5. Copy the whole `glyphs/` folder into `src/main/assets/` (the same place you put the fonts).

### 3.2 What to do if you need *no* glyphs at all  

If you truly want **zero** network traffic and you are happy with *all* scripts being drawn from TTFs, you can still keep an empty glyph tree:

```
assets/
 └─ glyphs/
     └─ .keep   (any empty file so the folder exists)
```

Then set the style’s `glyphs` field to the same `file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`.  
When the engine asks for a range that does not exist, it receives a 404-like error from the local file system; MapLibre Native treats that as “glyph not found” and **falls back to the `font-faces` entry** (or to the system default if none matches). This is safe and keeps the map functional.

> **Why not just omit `glyphs`?**  
> Native does not have the GL-JS “local-fonts-only” fallback (see the skill’s “GL JS only” note). The style must contain a `glyphs` field, otherwise the style is considered invalid and the map will not render any symbol layers.

---

## 4. Load the offline style in Android  

```kotlin
class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var mapView: MapView
    private lateinit var mapLibreMap: MapLibreMap

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        // 1️⃣ Inflate a layout that contains a MapView
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_map)
        mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView)

        // 2️⃣ Initialise the SDK (once per process)
        MapLibre.getInstance(this)

        // 3️⃣ Load the style JSON from assets (or from a raw resource)
        val styleJson = assets.open("style/offline-style.json")
            .bufferedReader()
            .use { it.readText() }

        // 4️⃣ Create the map and set the style
        mapView.getMapAsync { map ->
            mapLibreMap = map
            map.setStyle(
                Style.Builder()
                    .fromJson(styleJson)          // our JSON from step 2
            ) { style ->
                // style is ready – you can add sources, layers, etc.
                // No network calls will be made for glyphs or fonts.
            }
        }
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        mapView.onStart()
    }
    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        mapView.onStop()
    }
    // … (forward the other lifecycle callbacks)
}
```

* `Style.Builder().fromJson(styleJson)` parses the JSON exactly as MapLibre GL JS would.  
* Because the `glyphs` URL points at `file:///android_asset/...`, the SDK reads the PBF files directly from the APK.  
* Because the `font-faces` URLs also point at `file:///android_asset/...`, the native text-shaping engine loads the TTF/OTF files from the same bundle.  

No network traffic is required after the APK is installed.

---

|--------|--------------------------------

I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## Short answer **Yes – you can reuse the same `font-faces` block in a MapLibre GL JS style, but you have to meet a few extra requirements that are specific to the browser environment.** If those requirements are satisfied the result is the same “offline-font” behaviour you already have in Native: the browser loads the font files you point at, respects the `unicode-range` you declared, and the map draws every label from those local files instead of asking a glyph-PBF server. Below is a step-by-step checklist, the minimal code you need, and the gotchas that often trip people up when they copy a Native `font-faces` config straight into a web app. --- ## 1️⃣ What the spec says (and what GL JS actually implements) | Feature | MapLibre Native | MapLibre GL JS | |---------|----------------|----------------| | **`font-faces` property** | Read since Android 11.13.0 / iOS 6.18.0. Provides font files + optional `unicode-range`. | Read since **v6.7.0**. The same JSON shape is parsed. Fonts are fetched through the browser (or a Service Worker). | | **Runtime changes** | Not applicable (style is static). | `map.setFontFaces()` lets you replace the whole block after the map is created. | | **Fallback when `glyphs` is missing** | **Not supported** – Native still expects a glyph URL (open issue #165). | **Supported** since GL JS v5.11.0 – if `glyphs` is omitted or a particular PBF fails to load, GL JS falls back to the local-font path (TinySDF) and treats `text-font` as a CSS-style font-family list. | | **CJK handling** | Controlled by `localIdeographFontFamily` (default on). | Same, but the default is also “render locally”. | | **Right-to-left / complex shaping** | Uses HarfBuzz + `font-faces`. | Since v6.9.0 the browser’s text engine does shaping; `font-faces` supplies the font files. No RTL plugin needed. | > **Bottom line:** The JSON you already have is *valid* for GL JS, but the way the files are fetched is different (browser vs. native file system), and you must make sure the URLs are reachable **offline** (e.g. bundled with the app or cached by a Service Worker). --- ## 2️⃣ Checklist for a successful copy-paste | ✅ Item | Why it matters | How to satisfy it | |--------|----------------|-------------------| | **GL JS version ≥ 6.7.0** | Earlier versions ignore `font-faces`. | `npm i maplibre-gl@^6.7.0` (or later). | | **`glyphs` field** | GL JS will still try to fetch glyph PBFs for any codepoint that is *not* covered by a `font-faces` entry. If you want a pure-offline map, either:
• Omit `glyphs` entirely (local-font mode), **or**
• Point it at a dummy endpoint that returns 404 for every request (the fallback will kick in). | ```json "glyphs": "https://example.com/does-not-exist/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" ``` or simply remove the property. | | **Font URLs must be HTTP(S) reachable** | The browser cannot read a file on the device’s filesystem directly. | • Host the `.ttf/.otf` files on the same origin as your page (e.g. `./fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf`).
• Or embed them as **data-URI** strings (large but works offline). | | **CORS / `crossorigin`** | If you host fonts on a different origin, the request must allow cross-origin access, otherwise the font will be blocked and the map will fall back to the generic system font. | Set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) on the font server, or keep the fonts on the same origin. | | **Service-Worker caching (optional but recommended)** | To truly be offline you need the font files cached before the user loses connectivity. | In your SW `fetch` handler, `cache.put(request, response.clone())` for any `*.ttf`/`*.otf` request, or use `workbox-precaching`. | | **`unicode-range` syntax** | GL JS respects the same `unicode-range` array you already have. | Keep the exact same array (e.g. `["U+0900-097F"]`). | | **`localIdeographFontFamily`** (CJK) | If you keep the default, CJK characters are rendered locally with TinySDF and **ignore** the `text-font` list. | Either leave it as default (`'sans-serif'`) or set it to a specific on-device CJK font you bundle. | | **Testing** | Verify that the map works with the network disabled. | Open DevTools → Network → Offline, reload the page, and confirm that all labels still appear. | --- ## 3️⃣ Minimal example – copy-paste from Native to GL JS ### 3.1 Your existing Native `font-faces` (simplified) ```json { "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Regular": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF"] } ], "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] } } ``` ### 3.2 Adapted for the web ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://example.com/does-not-exist/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", // or omit entirely "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Regular": [ { "url": "./fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF"] } ], "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { "url": "./fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"], "text-size": 12 } } ] } ``` **Key changes** * `url` now points to a *relative* HTTP URL (`./fonts/...`). * `glyphs` points at a dead endpoint (or you can delete the property). * No `file://` scheme – browsers cannot read that. ### 3.3 Loading the style in GL JS ```javascript import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: '/styles/offline-fonts.json', // the JSON above center: [77.2, 28.6], zoom: 10, // optional – if you want a nicer CJK fallback: // localIdeographFontFamily: '"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif' }); // If you need to replace the block later (e.g. after a language switch): // map.setFontFaces(newFontFacesObject); ``` --- ## 4️⃣ Common pitfalls & how to fix them | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **All labels appear in a generic system font** | Font file failed to load (404, CORS, or blocked by mixed-content). | Open the Network tab, look for the `.ttf/.otf` request. Ensure the URL is correct, the server returns `200`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` includes your page origin. | | **CJK characters look blocky or disappear** | `localIdeographFontFamily` set to `false` *and* you have no CJK glyph PBFs. | Either remove `localIdeographFontFamily: false` (let TinySDF generate them) or provide a CJK font via `font-faces` and set `localIdeographFontFamily` to that family name. | | **Arabic text is garbled or shows reversed order** | Using a GL JS version < 6.9.0 *or* still loading the old RTL plugin. | Upgrade to ≥ 6.9.0 and **remove** any `setRTLTextPlugin` call. | | **Labels disappear only when the network is offline** | Fonts are not cached. | Add the font URLs to your Service Worker precache list (e.g. with Workbox) or use the `Cache` API manually. | | **`unicode-range` seems ignored (extra characters appear in the wrong font)** | The range string is malformed (e.g. missing `U+`). | Follow the spec exactly: `"unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]`. No spaces, uppercase `U`. | | **`font-faces` is ignored completely** | GL JS version < 6.7.0 or the style is loaded *before* the map is created and you later call `map.setFontFaces()` with a different object that overwrites it. | Verify `maplibre-gl` version, and only call `setFontFaces` **after** the map is instantiated if you need to change it. | --- ## 5️⃣ Offline-first workflow (recommended) 1. **Bundle the fonts** with your web app (e.g. `public/fonts/…`). 2. **Add them to the Service Worker precache** (Workbox example below). ```javascript // workbox-config.js module.exports = { globDirectory: 'public/', globPatterns: [ '**/*.{html,js,css}', 'fonts/*.ttf', 'styles/*.json' ], swDest: 'public/sw.js', }; ``` 3. **Deploy the SW** and register it in your page: ```javascript if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) { navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js'); } ``` Now the browser will serve the font files from the cache even when the user is completely offline, and the map will continue to render exactly the same way as your Native app. --- ## 6️⃣ TL;DR summary * **Yes** – copy the `font-faces` block into your GL JS style. * Use GL JS ≥ 6.7.0. * Change the `url`s from `file://…` (Native) to **HTTP(S) URLs** that the browser can fetch (relative to your site, CDN, or data-URI). * Either **omit `glyphs`** or point it at a dead endpoint so the map never tries to download glyph PBFs. * Ensure the fonts are **CORS-accessible** and **cached** (Service Worker) if you truly need offline operation. * For CJK you can keep the default `localIdeographFontFamily` (fast, no glyphs). * For Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, etc., the `font-faces` entries supply the correct font files; GL JS will use the browser’s shaping engine automatically (no RTL plugin needed). Follow the checklist, test with the network throttled/offline, and you’ll get the same deterministic, offline-font rendering you already enjoy in MapLibre Native. Happy mapping!

Choose a font * **Noto Sans Arabic** – covers Arabic, Persian, Urdu, etc. * **Noto Sans Hebrew** – covers Hebrew and Yiddish. * Any other OpenType font that includes the required Unicode ranges (U+0590-U+05FF for Hebrew, U+0600-U+06FF for Arabic, plus the extended Arabic-Supplement blocks). ### 2.2. Make the font reachable to MapLibre You have **two** ways to make the font available: | Method | When to use it | How it works | |--------|----------------|--------------| | **`glyphs` URL** (pre-generated SDF PBFs) | You already have a glyph server (e.g. `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) and you want the same look on every device. | The style’s `glyphs` field points to the server; `text-font` names must match the folder names on the server (`"Noto Sans Arabic"` etc.). | | **`font-faces`** (direct TTF/OTF loading) | You want to avoid a glyph server, want offline support, or you need a custom brand font. | The style’s root `font-faces` object maps a `text-font` name to one or more `url` entries (TTF/OTF). The browser loads the font file and the GL JS text engine draws the characters directly. | #### 2.2.1. Using `font-faces` (recommended for RTL scripts) Add a `font-faces` block to your style JSON (or set it at runtime with `map.setFontFaces()`). ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", // can stay, it will be ignored for Arabic/Hebrew "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF", "U+FB50-FDFF", "U+FE70-FEFF", "U+1EE00-1EEFF"] } ], "Noto Sans Hebrew": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0590-05FF", "U+FB1D-FB4F"] } ] }, "layers": [ … ] } ``` *The `unicode-range` entries are optional but help the engine know which file to use for which code points.* If you prefer to set it **after** the map is created (e.g. you load fonts lazily), you can do: ```js map.setFontFaces({ "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF"] } ], "Noto Sans Hebrew": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0590-05FF"] } ] }); ``` > **Note for Native** – The same `font-faces` block works on MapLibre Native (Android ≥ 11.13.0, iOS ≥ 6.18.0). The server is only a fallback for characters that the browser cannot render. --- ## 3. Reference the font in your label layers Every `symbol` layer that shows Arabic or Hebrew text must list the font name in its `text-font` property. The property is an **ordered fallback list** – the first font that contains the needed glyphs wins. ```json { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], // assumes the OSM `name` field contains Arabic/Hebrew strings "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Arabic", // try Arabic first "Noto Sans Hebrew", // then Hebrew "Noto Sans Regular" // fallback for Latin, etc. ], "text-size": 12, "text-direction": "auto", // optional – lets the engine decide per-label "text-anchor": "center" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ``` ### Why the order matters * If a label contains only Arabic characters, the engine will pick **Noto Sans Arabic**. * If a label contains only Hebrew characters, it will fall back to **Noto Sans Hebrew**. * If a label mixes scripts (e.g., Arabic + Latin), the first font that covers each code point is used for that character. ## Why the Devanagari text looks “letter-by-letter” Devanagari (Hindi) is a **complex-script** language: a base consonant can combine with vowel signs, diacritics, and conjuncts that must be **shaped** together as a single grapheme cluster. * When a style points at a `glyphs` URL, MapLibre GL JS used to fetch a separate SDF glyph for **each code-point**. * That works fine for simple Latin, Arabic, etc., but it cannot render the required ligatures for Devanagari – the browser receives three independent SDF images and they end up stacked incorrectly. Since **MapLibre GL JS v6.7.0** the engine draws those scripts with the **browser’s text engine** (via `font-faces`) instead of the glyph PBFs, and from **v6.15.0** it does it for **every** code-point in the cluster. If you are still seeing the “each letter on its own” artefact, one (or more) of the following is true: | Situation | What’s happening | Fix | |-----------|------------------|-----| | **Using a version < 6.7.0** | Only the glyph-PBF path is used → no shaping. | Upgrade to at least **v6.15.0** (latest stable). | | **`font-faces` not declared or the font file cannot be loaded** | The browser falls back to the glyph-PBF path (or to a generic system font) → wrong shaping. | Add a `font-faces` entry that points to a Devanagari-capable TTF/OTF (e.g. Noto Sans Devanagari) and make sure the URL is reachable. | | **`glyphs` URL is present but the Devanagari PBFs are still being requested** | GL JS will still request the PBFs, but they are ignored for shaping; however if the `font-faces` entry is missing the fallback is the PBF → wrong rendering. | Keep the `glyphs` URL (it’s fine) **but** also supply `font-faces`. | | **CORS / loading error for the TTF/OTF** | Browser blocks the font, so GL JS reverts to the glyph PBFs. | Ensure the font file is served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) and that the MIME type is `font/ttf` / `font/otf`. | Below is a step-by-step recipe that works for any modern MapLibre GL JS map. --- ## 1. Upgrade MapLibre GL JS ```html ``` *If you already use a bundler, bump the `maplibre-gl` dependency to `^6.15.0` (or newer).* --- ## 2. Add a `font-faces` block to your style ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://my-tileserver.example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { "url": "https://my-tileserver.example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels-hi", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "filter": ["==", "$type", "Point"], "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name:hi"], "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"], "text-size": 12 }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ] } ``` ### Key points | Property | Why it matters | |----------|----------------| | **`font-faces` name** (`"Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"`) | Must **exactly** match the first entry in the `text-font` array. | | **`url`** | Must be a **direct URL** that the browser can fetch (CORS-enabled). | | **`unicode-range`** | Limits the file to Devanagari code points; optional but recommended. | | **`text-font` fallback** | Keep a generic fallback (`"Noto Sans Regular"` or `"sans-serif"`) for any characters outside the range. | > **Tip:** If you already have the Noto Sans Devanagari TTF on disk, you can host it on the same origin as your style (e.g. `/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf`). That avoids cross-origin headaches. --- ## 3. (Optional) Tell GL JS to use the same `font-faces` at runtime If you need to change the font set after the map is created (e.g., a UI that lets the user pick a different Devanagari font), call: ```js map.setFontFaces({ "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { url: "https://my-tileserver.example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] }); ``` The call can be made **once**, before any layers that use the font are added, or anytime you want to replace the mapping. --- ## 4. Verify that the font is actually being used Open the browser’s **Network** tab and look for a request like: ``` GET https://my-tileserver.example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf ``` You should see a **200** response with `content-type: font/ttf` (or `font/otf`). If you only see requests for `.../{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` and **no** TTF request, the `font-faces` entry is either miss-spelled or blocked by CORS. --- ## 5. (If you still see problems) Double-check the text source * Ensure the `name:hi` property in your source actually contains **Unicode Devanagari** characters, not Latin transliteration. * Verify that the string is **normalized** (NFC) – most OSM data is already NFC, but if you generate labels yourself, run `String.prototype.normalize()` before feeding them to the style. ```js const label = feature.properties['name:hi'].normalize('NFC'); ``` --- ## 6. Keep the `glyphs` URL – it’s still useful * The `glyphs` endpoint is still consulted for **simple scripts** (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc.) and for **fallback characters** that are not covered by any `font-faces` entry. * For Devanagari you can even point the `glyphs` URL at a **dummy** server (or leave it as the default) – it will never be used for shaping, but keeping it avoids style-validation errors. --- ## 7. Full minimal example (HTML) ```html MapLibre – Hindi labels
``` Open the page, zoom in on a Hindi-named place (e.g., “दिल्ली”), and you should see the vowel signs and conjuncts correctly positioned. --- ## TL;DR Checklist 1. **Upgrade** to MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.15.0. 2. **Add** a `font-faces` entry for the Devanagari font (TTF/OTF) with the correct `unicode-range`. 3. **Make sure** the font URL is CORS-enabled and reachable. 4. **Reference** that exact name as the first entry in `text-font`. 5. **Keep** the `glyphs` URL (it won’t be used for Devanagari but is harmless). 6. **Test** that the TTF request appears in the network tab and that Hindi labels render with proper ligatures. Below is a minimal, step-by-step recipe for adding a **hillshade** layer that draws from a **raster-DEM** source in a MapLibre GL JS map. You can copy-paste the code, adapt the URLs and layer styling, and you’ll see a shaded relief surface over your base map. --- ## 1. Prerequisites | What you need | Why | |---------------|-----| | **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 1.15** (or any recent version) | Hillshade support was added early on and is stable. | | A **raster-DEM** tile service (e.g. a Mapbox Terrain-RGB, a custom MBTiles server, or any XYZ source that returns 16-bit elevation tiles) | The hillshade layer reads elevation values from these tiles. | | CORS enabled on the DEM endpoint (or proxy) | The browser must be allowed to fetch the tiles. | | (Optional) A **style** that already contains a base raster or vector layer – you’ll be adding the hillshade on top of it. | Gives you something to compare against. | --- ## 2. Add the DEM source to the style ```javascript // 1️⃣ Create the map (replace with your own container / options) const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', // HTML element id style: 'https://demotiles.maplibre.org/style.json', // any base style center: [-122.447303, 37.753574], // lon, lat zoom: 12 }); // 2️⃣ When the style is loaded, add the raster-DEM source map.on('style.load', () => { map.addSource('dem', { type: 'raster-dem', // Example: Mapbox Terrain-RGB (public demo tiles) // Replace with your own DEM endpoint if you have one. url: 'https://api.maptiler.com/tiles/terrain-rgb/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=YOUR_MAPTILER_KEY', // If you serve your own tiles, use the XYZ template instead: // url: 'https://myserver.com/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png', tileSize: 256, // most DEM tiles are 256 px // The DEM values are encoded as 16-bit RGB; tell MapLibre to decode them: encoding: 'terrarium' // or 'mapbox' for Mapbox Terrain-RGB }); ``` **Key points** * `type: 'raster-dem'` tells MapLibre that the source contains elevation data, not imagery. * `encoding` must match how the DEM tiles are encoded: * `'mapbox'` – Mapbox Terrain-RGB (default for Mapbox tiles). * `'terrarium'` – Terrarium format (used by many open-source DEM providers). * `tileSize` is usually 256 px; set to 512 only if your tiles are that size. --- ## 3. Add the hillshade layer ```javascript // 3️⃣ Add the hillshade layer *after* the DEM source map.addLayer({ id: 'hillshade', type: 'hillshade', source: 'dem', // reference the source we just added // Optional: limit the hillshade to a specific zoom range minzoom: 0, maxzoom: 22, paint: { // These are the default values – tweak them to taste 'hillshade-illumination-direction': 335, // sun azimuth (degrees) 'hillshade-illumination-anchor': 'map', // 'map' (fixed) or 'viewport' (moves with camera) 'hillshade-exaggeration': 0.5, // vertical exaggeration (1 = true scale) 'hillshade-shadow-color': '#000000', 'hillshade-highlight-color': '#ffffff', 'hillshade-accent-color': '#000000' // optional, for subtle accent lines } }); }); ``` ### What the paint properties do | Property | Typical range | Effect | |----------|---------------|--------| | `hillshade-illumination-direction` | 0-360° | Sun azimuth; rotate to change shadow direction. | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | `'map'` or `'viewport'` | `'map'` keeps the sun fixed to the map; `'viewport'` makes the light follow the camera. | | `hillshade-exaggeration` | 0-2 (or higher) | Scales the vertical relief; >1 makes mountains look steeper. | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | any CSS color | Color of shadows / highlights. | | `hillshade-accent-color` | any CSS color | Optional thin lines that emphasize terrain ridges. | You can animate the sun direction, change exaggeration with a UI slider, or bind it to the map’s pitch/rotation for a “dynamic lighting” effect. --- ## 4. (Optional) Put the hillshade under or over other layers By default `addLayer` inserts the new layer **above** all existing layers. If you want the hillshade **below** your base raster or vector tiles, pass a third argument: ```javascript // Insert hillshade just above the "water" layer, but below everything else map.addLayer(hillshadeLayerObject, 'water'); ``` Or, after the map is loaded, reorder: ```javascript map.moveLayer('hillshade', 'road-label'); // move it just below road labels ``` --- ## 5. Full working example (HTML) ```html MapLibre GL JS – Hillshade from raster-DEM
``` *Replace `YOUR_MAPTILER_KEY` with a valid API key (or point `url` at your own DEM tiles).* --- ## 6. Common pitfalls & troubleshooting | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **No hillshade appears** (map stays flat) | DEM source not loading (404, CORS, wrong URL) | Open the network tab, verify tile requests succeed. Ensure the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*` (or your domain). | | **Hillshade looks completely white or black** | Wrong `encoding` value (e.g., using `'terrarium'` for Mapbox Terrain-RGB) | Set `encoding` to `'mapbox'` for Terrain-RGB, `'terrarium'` for Terrarium tiles. | | **Shadows are in the wrong direction** | `hillshade-illumination-direction` not set or set to default (335°) | Adjust the azimuth value (0-360°) to match the desired sun position. | | **Tile loading is very slow** | Using a public DEM endpoint with rate limits or high latency | Cache tiles locally, use a CDN, or host your own DEM tiles. | | **Hillshade disappears when zooming out** | `maxzoom`/`minzoom` on the layer or source too restrictive | Remove or increase the zoom limits. | | **CORS error in console** | DEM server does not allow cross-origin requests | Add appropriate CORS headers on the server, or proxy the tiles through a same-origin endpoint. | --- ## 7. Going further * **Dynamic sun** – Listen to `move` events and update `hillshade-illumination-direction` based on map bearing or time of day. * **Terrain 3-D** – If you also want true 3-D extrusion, add a `terrain` source (`map.addSource('terrain', {type: 'raster-dem', ...})`) and set `map.setTerrain({source: 'terrain', exaggeration: 1.5});`. Hillshade works nicely together with 3-D terrain. * **Multiple DEM sources** – You can add more than one DEM source (e.g., higher-resolution tiles for a city) and switch between them with `setStyle` or `setPaintProperty` on the hillshade layer. --- ### TL;DR 1. **Add a `raster-dem` source** (point it at your DEM tiles, set `encoding`). 2. **Add a `hillshade` layer** that references that source and optionally tweak its paint properties. 3. **Adjust layer order** if you need the hillshade under/over other layers. 4. **Check CORS and encoding** if nothing shows up. That’s all you need to get a shaded-relief layer onto any MapLibre GL JS map. Happy mapping!
